lessons.title: Two Mindsets, Two Different Worlds
lessons.key_idea: Whether you believe ability is fixed or can grow changes how you interpret almost every challenge you face.

lessons.title: Failure as Verdict or as Information
lessons.key_idea: A fixed mindset treats setbacks and effort as proof of inadequacy, while a growth mindset treats them as the path to improvement.

lessons.title: The Myth of Natural Talent
lessons.key_idea: Even celebrated stars in sports and other fields became great through practice and learning, not talent alone.

lessons.title: Praise the Process, Not the Person
lessons.key_idea: Praising intelligence makes people avoid challenges, while praising effort and strategy makes them seek challenges and persist.

lessons.title: Leaders Who Learn Versus Leaders Who Prove
lessons.key_idea: Fixed-mindset leaders need to look superior and silence bad news, while growth-mindset leaders build teams that learn and adapt.

lessons.title: Mindsets in Love and Friendship
lessons.key_idea: Believing good relationships should be effortless makes problems feel fatal, while a growth mindset sees conflict as something partners can work through.

lessons.title: How to Change Your Mindset
lessons.key_idea: You can shift toward growth by noticing your fixed-mindset voice, answering it, and treating every skill as not yet mastered rather than impossible.

plan.title: Mindset
plan.author: Carol S. Dweck
plan.confidence_note: I know this book's core arguments, structure and main examples well, though I'd avoid fine-grained details like exact study figures.
plan.one_liner: Your beliefs about whether ability can grow quietly shape how you learn, fail, lead and love.
plan.summary: Psychologist Carol Dweck argues that people hold one of two broad beliefs about their abilities. In a fixed mindset, talent and intelligence are set traits, so every challenge becomes a test of worth and failure feels like a verdict. In a growth mindset, abilities can be developed through effort, good strategies and help from others, so challenges become chances to learn. Drawing on decades of research and examples from school, sports, business and relationships, Dweck shows how these mindsets shape whether people seek challenges, persist through setbacks, accept feedback and celebrate others' success. She explains how praise, parenting, teaching and leadership can push people toward one mindset or the other. Most importantly, she argues that mindsets themselves can change, and offers practical ways to notice your fixed-mindset voice and choose growth instead.
